events.text: Most people think the smart way to learn business is a degree.

card.text: $0 vs an MBA: what actually helps in year one?

events.text: For a new small business in Canada, the opposite is often true.

card.text: $0 vs an MBA: what actually helps in year one?

card.text: $0 vs an MBA: what actually helps in year one?

One is a free visit from the tax people that is not an audit.
One is a course that Nova Scotia requires in every food business.
And one popular marketing certificate that a lot of people assume is free actually charges you for the exam.
Let's go through what's worth your time, what isn't, and what to do this week.

events.text: First, what a business degree actually gives you.
An M B A teaches the big frames.
Finance, accounting, marketing, operations, strategy.
You learn to read a balance sheet and think about a whole company.
That's real value.
It also comes with a network and a credential that employers recognise.
If you want to climb inside a big organisation, it can matter a lot.
But here's the part school doesn't spend much time on.

events.text: Before the free stuff, one number that changes how you should think about all of this.

A big company sends one person to learn tax rules and another to learn advertising.
A three person company sends the owner to learn all of it.

events.text: And for some businesses, one of these isn't optional at all.
If you run a café, a food truck, a bakery, anything that serves food, this one is for you.
As of November twenty twenty six, Nova Scotia's food safety regulations require at least one person per shift who has completed a food hygiene course.

card.title: Nova Scotia food establishments
card.text: At least one person per shift must have completed a food hygiene (handling) course. Renew every 5 years.

events.text: For a small business, the useful part isn't the badge at all.
It's that the course walks you through the exact reports that tell you where your website visitors come from, which pages they leave from, and whether that flyer or that ad did anything.
Next, HubSpot Academy, which describes itself as free, self paced training.
Its marketing courses are popular with small business owners because they teach the whole funnel.
How people find you, why they trust you, and how they end up paying.
Two honest catches.
HubSpot says certifications expire, one year for its software certifications and two years for the others.
And its terms say it could choose to charge for certifications at any time.
You can retake an exam as many times as you want, twelve hours apart.
So failing once costs you nothing but a bit of pride.
Now, the one I promised.
Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram.
Its Blueprint courses are free to study.
But the official Meta certification exam is paid.
One recent guide lists the associate exam at ninety nine U S dollars, and says to check the live price before you pay.
So if a post tells you all the big marketing certificates are free, that's not quite right.
The learning is free.
The badge sometimes isn't.
Here's the uncomfortable part, though.
None of these certificates will get you a single customer by themselves.
A certificate on your wall does nothing for a customer standing at your counter.
What they notice is whether you showed up when you said, whether the invoice made sense, whether your shop shows up when they search.
This is the gap between school and the real thing.
